title: Visiting the sick
hook: no harm, a purification, if Allah wills (Bukhari)
tomorrow: someone sneezes mid-visit. is there a right thing to say?

segments.voice: Yesterday, beneficial rain: not more of a thing, the good kind of it. Today, a harder kind of weather, the kind inside a body.

The hospital door is half open. There's a beeping machine, a tray of food nobody touched, and someone you love looking smaller than usual in a gown. You hover in the doorway holding a card. Everything you rehearsed sounds wrong now. Get well soon feels thin. Everything happens for a reason feels worse. Al-Bukhari keeps a scene for exactly this doorway. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, visits a sick man, a Bedouin, and says a few short words: no harm, a purification, if God wills. And the man argues back.
screen: `THE DOOR IS HALF OPEN.` → `GET WELL SOON FEELS THIN.` → `NO HARM, A PURIFICATION.` → `THE MAN ARGUES BACK.`

segments.voice: A purification, says the Bedouin? No. It's a fever boiling in an old man, and it will take him to the grave. And the Prophet answers: then so it is. He doesn't win the point. The words of comfort are offered, not forced, and the sick man's own account is allowed to stand. That's the first lesson of the room: say the hopeful thing, then listen. Now the debate, and it's a real one. Is visiting the sick a duty, or a strongly urged kindness? One view: a duty. The Prophet told his followers to feed the hungry, visit the sick and free the captive, in the form of a command, and al-Bukhari himself names a chapter for the obligation of visiting the sick. The other view: it's urged so strongly that a community must see it done, but not every person sins by missing one visit; someone goes, and the duty is met. Both views send people through that doorway. Neither treats it as optional in spirit. And here's why. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, God says on the last day: I was sick and you did not visit Me. How could You be sick? the person asks. And God answers: had you visited him, you would have found Me with him. Christians know a close neighbor of this line, from Matthew's Gospel: "I was sick, and ye visited me."
screen: `SAY THE HOPEFUL THING, THEN LISTEN.` · `VIEW ONE: A DUTY.` · `VIEW TWO: STRONGLY URGED, ON THE COMMUNITY.` · `YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.` · then, large: `A PURIFICATION.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who is unwell right now, in body or in spirit. Write them a short message, three or four plain lines, no advice. You can send it after the sit, or keep it as a draft until it feels right.
screen: `ONE PERSON WHO IS UNWELL.` · `A SHORT MESSAGE, NO ADVICE.`

segments.voice: Visiting the sick. In Arabic, 'iyadat al-marid: going to someone who is ill, a deed so urged that scholars debate whether it's a duty.
Hold onto this: a purification, offered gently, and then you listen. Day thirteen of fourteen remembrances.

screen: `DAY 1613 COUNTS.` → `DAILY REMEMBRANCES · 13 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: SOMEONE SNEEZES. NOW WHAT?`

howItsDone: Muslims visit the sick at home and in hospitals, often saying the Prophet's words from al-Bukhari, la ba's, tahurun in sha Allah: no harm, a purification, if God wills.

fork.setup: your friend says visiting the sick is a strict duty for every Muslim, every time. she asks for the best case for the other view. what do you give her?
options: it's just a nice extra; the Prophet never really told anyone to do it.
it's urged so strongly the community must see it done, and when someone goes, the duty is met.
visiting doesn't help the patient, so it can't be a duty.
fork.reveal: that's the strongest form of the second view. the first view points to the command to visit the sick and al-Bukhari's chapter on its obligation. both send people through the door.

original.note: Arabic: tahur, a purification. From the visit: la ba's, tahurun in sha Allah.

what a scholar hears: an open question whether 'iyadat al-marid is an individual duty or a communal one; al-Bukhari's chapter title calls it an obligation, and the hadith in Muslim finds God with the sick.

options: Scholars differ: a duty, or so urged someone must go. Either way, the Prophet went himself.

Required, but only if you say the Arabic words at the bed, or it doesn't count.
chat.meaning: Some scholars call visiting the sick a duty; others say it's urged so strongly the community must see it done. The Prophet visited, and said: a purification.

notes: Bukhari 3616/5656 paraphrased: the Bedouin's reply ('a fever boiling in an old man that will take him to the grave') and the Prophet's 'then so it is' (na'am idhan). Confirm numbers and that the paraphrase is fair.

Debate: some scholars held visiting the sick an individual obligation (al-Bukhari titles a chapter 'wujub 'iyadat al-marid' in Kitab al-Marda); others held it sunnah mu'akkadah or a communal obligation (fard kifaya). The voice does not say which view is larger. Confirm the chapter title and fair statement of both views.
